summary: Traced the 5-link E-E-A-T trust chain for utilityexplained.com. Result: 1 HOLDS, 3 WEAK, 1 BROKEN. The disclosure architecture genuinely holds (every monetized page either carries the affiliate-disclosure shortcode or the product-box shortcode self-discloses 'may earn a commission'). The chain breaks most severely on author identity: all 5 author pages are explicitly 'editorial bylines' for desks (not identifiable credentialed individuals), with zero credentials anywhere. Sources coverage is structurally strong (84/88 posts carry a sources field) but only ~40 of those 84 carry an explicit retrieval date — falling short of the editorial-policy's own promise of 'dated source links'. The corrections page is a policy statement with no demonstrated corrections history (no log entries anywhere in content/). Eight specific unsupported claim lines were quoted, concentrated in buying-guide savings tables and the 2026 state-cost data page.
findings: LINK 1 — AUTHOR IDENTITY: WEAK. All 5 author pages exist and the editorial-team.md page matches all 5 (content/editorial-team.md lists each of the 5 editors with matching roles). Byline coverage is total: all 88 blog posts carry an author field (grep: 46 Margaret Harrington, 16 Tanya Patterson, 12 Roberto Mendoza, 8 David Chen, 6 Marcia Washington; 0 posts with no author). BUT every author page explicitly declares the name is a desk brand, not a person: 'David Chen is the editorial byline for Utility Explained's Energy Efficiency desk. It identifies the desk responsible for...' (content/author/david-chen.md), and the identical 'is the editorial byline for...desk' formula appears on all 5 author pages (marcia-washington.md, margaret-harrington.md, roberto-mendoza.md, tanya-patterson.md). Zero credentials on any author page — grep for degree/license/certified/engineer/experience returned nothing across content/author/. The team page is transparent about AI: 'Guides may use AI assistance during drafting. That assistance is not evidence' (content/editorial-team.md) and each author page carries the same AI-disclosure footnote. A skeptical reader finds an honest AI disclosure but no verifiable human expertise behind the named bylines, and the pages themselves admit the names are editorial constructs. Weakest link on identity = no credential, no real-person verification, though disclosure is honest.

LINK 2 — EDITORIAL PROMISES vs PRACTICE: WEAK. The editorial-policy promises 'direct, dated source links for their material figures and claims' (content/editorial-policy.md line 34) and 'Material updates carry a visible Updated date' (line 42). Practice: 84/88 blog posts (95%) carry a 'sources:' front-matter field — strong coverage. BUT of those 84, only 40 posts contain an explicit retrieval-date token anywhere in the post ('retrieved 2026-08-28' or 'as of 2026-08-28' — e.g., content/blog/03-why-is-my-electric-bill-so-high.md:18 'retrieved 2026-08-28'). The other ~44 posts list bare URLs with no retrieval date — failing the policy's own 'dated source links' promise. The 4 posts with NO sources field are substantive guides with zero URLs: ac-running-but-not-cooling.md, aux-heat-vs-emergency-heat-meaning.md, heat-pump-running-all-day-in-winter.md, mcf-vs-ccf-vs-therms-on-gas-bill.md. The layout DOES render the updated/reviewed date (layouts/_default/single.html renders 'Reviewed: <time>' from .Params.updated), so update-dating is honored in the template. Net: sources present but only ~48% dated; the policy overpromises what the pages deliver.

LINK 3 — DISCLOSURE ARCHITECTURE: HOLDS. The affiliate-disclosure shortcode (layouts/shortcodes/affiliate-disclosure.html) renders a compliant FTC disclosure: 'Disclosure: Some links in this article are affiliate links. If you buy through them, we may earn a small commission...As an Amazon Associate, we earn from qualifying purchases.' The standalone affiliate-disclosure.md page exists and states revenue model ('our primary revenue is display advertising. On product-focused guides, we also use affiliate links...As an Amazon Associate we earn from qualifying purchases'). Coverage: 38/88 posts carry the shortcode. 26 posts carry product-box; of those 26, 5 lack the standalone shortcode (11-understanding-kwh-usage.md, 46-what-time-is-electricity-cheapest.md, how-do-smart-meters-work.md, how-to-lower-electric-bill-without-solar.md, why-did-my-water-bill-suddenly-increase.md) — BUT the product-box shortcode itself self-discloses inline: 'Price & availability shown on Amazon.com — we may earn a commission' with rel='sponsored nofollow noopener' (layouts/shortcodes/product-box.html). So every monetized page carries a visible disclosure either via shortcode or via the box's own inline note. A reader on any commercial page can identify the monetization. This is the strongest link.

LINK 4 — RECOURSE (contact & corrections): WEAK. Contact is genuinely usable: content/contact.md provides a working mailto (hello@utilityexplained.com, line 27). The corrections page (content/corrections.md) states a real policy: how to report (contact), what happens next (review against sources; 'if the content is wrong, we correct it promptly'; 'for significant corrections, we note what changed'). BUT there is no demonstrated corrections history anywhere in content/ — grep for 'corrected'/'we corrected' across content/ returned only incidental uses (e.g., 'estimate correction' in 06-water-bill-too-high.md:136) and zero correction-log pages or dated correction entries. The policy page promises 'we note what changed' but the corpus contains no visible change-notes. A reader can reach a human and find a policy, but cannot verify that corrections ever actually happen — a trust gap for YMYL money content.

LINK 5 — CLAIM HYGIENE: WEAK. Across 88 posts the dominant pattern is honest, bracket-style sourcing ('Official ranges, properly separated: DOE says reducing drafts may save 5–30%... use them as brackets' — content/blog/47-check-energy-leaks-home-diy.md:107; and the 10%-setback figure is consistently attributed to DOE with [n] markers across 03/05/07/30/42/44). BUT 8 specific unsupported claim lines carry no citation marker at all in money-relevant contexts: (1) content/blog/average-utility-bills-by-state-2026.md:126 'In 2026, 12 states implemented new conservation-tier pricing' — specific factual claim, zero citation; (2) same line, 'drought surcharges of up to 30%' — zero citation; (3) content/blog/07-gas-bill-too-high.md:160 'Window film insulation kits...reduces heat loss by 40–70%' — no citation; (4) content/blog/07-gas-bill-too-high.md:161 'Thermal curtains...blocks drafts and radiant heat loss' — no citation; (5) content/blog/44-how-to-lower-water-bill.md:107 'Mulch 2–3 inches...20–30% reduction in watering frequency' — uncited table row; (6) content/blog/44-how-to-lower-water-bill.md:104 'Drip irrigation...30–50% reduction' — uncited; (7) content/blog/44-how-to-lower-water-bill.md:106 'Rain barrel...1,000–5,000 gal/yr' — uncited; (8) content/blog/05-how-to-lower-utility-bills.md:85 'Water heater insulation wrap...Reduces standby heat loss 25–45% per DOE' — attribution to DOE with no link and a suspect upper bound (DOE typically cites ~25% for electric wrap; the 45% figure needs its source). These sit in buying-guide decision tables where a reader choosing upgrades is exactly where a fabricated rate would matter. The narrative prose is well-cited; the tabular savings claims are the weak spots.

SOURCES-COVERAGE NOTE (supports Links 2 & 5): 84 of 88 posts carry a 'sources:' front-matter field; only ~40 of those 84 contain an explicit retrieval-date token ('retrieved 2026-08-28' / 'as of 2026-08-28'); zero uses of an 'accessed:' or 'retrieved:' YAML key (grep for '^(retrieved|accessed|as-of|last-reviewed)' returned 0 across content/blog/); 2 posts embed a dated archive.org snapshot URL (with 14-digit snapshot stamp); the 4 sources-less posts (ac-running-but-not-cooling, aux-heat-vs-emergency-heat-meaning, heat-pump-running-all-day-in-winter, mcf-vs-ccf-vs-therms-on-gas-bill) contain zero https URLs — even though the editorial-policy's published standard says pages without visible Sources should be treated as 'general educational context,' these are substantive how-to guides presented as current recommendations.

TOP-LEVEL VERDICT: This is a structurally conscientious utility-information site — total byline coverage, 95% sources coverage, honest AI disclosure, a genuinely FTC-compliant disclosure system, and a working contact path. It fails on the depth of that structure: author bylines are admitted desks with zero credentials, only ~half the sourced posts carry retrieval dates despite the policy promising them, and 8 specific unsupported claim lines sit in buying-decision savings tables. High-leverage fixes, cheapest first: (1) add inline retrieval dates to the ~44 dated-less sources blocks to meet the policy's own wording; (2) either flesh out the 5 bylines into identifiable people with credentials or rename them '[Name] Editorial Desk' to remove the person-impression the current 'editorial byline for...desk' wording creates; (3) create a dated corrections-log page listing actual past corrections — even a short list of the 8 claims above demonstrates the loop works. Fix those three and the chain flips to mostly HOLDS.
